findings.where: First screen, the email action 'Mark.Moseley@MMMinfra.com' (parts.txt p16)
findings.fault: The page's one action goes nowhere. Its link points to '#', not to a mailto: address, so clicking the white button does nothing. The address shows, but no email opens.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank officer who clicks to write to Mark gets nothing. The page exists so people can contact him, and its only action is dead.

findings.where: First screen, the five topic pills (PPP Law, Infrastructure, Development banks, Governments, Risk allocation; parts.txt p10–p14), desktop and phone
findings.fault: The pills do nothing, but they look like buttons or filters: each has a white outlined capsule and semibold sans labels on the blue field, a step down from the filled email button. They also add a row of parts on a first screen that should carry one message and one action. On a phone they take up three lines and push the action further down.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who clicks 'PPP Law' expecting his work on PPP law gets no response and decides the site is broken. The founder asked for one action on the first screen, and five button-like shapes compete with it.

findings.where: First screen, the blue field's ground (desktop-01, phone-01) against the Texture tile's own note (desktop-02, phone-02)
findings.fault: The field has fine diagonal stripes from edge to edge. The tile's own Texture panel shows a flat field and says 'No texture: one flat field, no grain and no gradient'. The direction is 'one blue field', and the stripes make the ground busy behind the large serif line and the body copy. They also look like hatching on a technical drawing.
findings.who_objects: The founder judges the first screen against the tile's own spec and the brief's 'one soft ground' and 'nothing in-your-face techy', and the striped field breaks all three. Mark has said he dislikes busy sites.

findings.where: First screen, the large ghost 'PPP' letters behind the heading (desktop-01). On a phone (phone-01) they are cut off at the right edge as a faint 'PP'
findings.fault: A huge pale 'PPP' sits behind Mark's line and overlaps 'In my view, we are at'. It is a second large typographic element fighting the one big line, an ornament the brief and the tile's notes never mention. On a phone it is cropped into a smudge that looks like a rendering fault.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for scale contrast from one very large serif line rather than more elements, and for a refined look with no novelty. A reader looking at the heading meets letters behind letters.

findings.where: Article specimen: the 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' link and the list bullets (desktop-04, phone-03)
findings.fault: The article brings in an orange-red that is in neither the house colours nor the tile's own palette. The palette panel says 'Four colours and no accent' and names house blue for links, yet this link is orange-red while 'Play again' further down is blue. Links on the page now come in two colours.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose brief makes the house blue and grey the only ink, will find a colour the tile says it does not have. A reader sees two link colours and cannot tell which one means 'link'.

findings.where: Article specimen: the three-item list (desktop-04, phone-03)
findings.fault: The list is set solid, with its lines almost touching. That is far tighter than the paragraphs' 19/30 rhythm, and the wrapped line 'Cycle.' crowds the item above it. The brief asked this specimen to show that the rhythm holds when Angélique adds a list, and here it breaks.
findings.who_objects: Angélique, who will add lists to articles and get cramped blocks. The founder, who set this exact test in the brief. A reader, for whom the list reads as a dense block in the middle of the article.

findings.where: Article specimen: the image caption and the subhead 'So, what are the key ‘chapter topics’?' (desktop-04, phone-03)
findings.fault: The subhead starts directly under the caption with no space above it, so the caption seems to belong to the subhead rather than the photo. The subhead is also as large and heavy as the article title (on a phone it is larger), so it competes with the title instead of sitting below it.
findings.who_objects: A reader of the article loses track of where the photo ends and the next section starts, and of which heading ranks higher. The founder asked for spacing on a rhythm that survives an image, a caption and a subhead being added.

findings.where: Header lockup, desktop and phone (desktop-01, phone-01)
findings.fault: The logo comes first and Mark's name sits second, to its right, in small type about the size of a nav label. The name does not lead.
findings.who_objects: The founder's personal-advisor test says his name leads, with the logo beside it. Here the firm's mark comes first and the person comes second.

findings.fault: On a phone the portrait comes first, at full width, above the heading. The first screen shows the header, the photo and its caption, and the start of Mark's line; the email action is about two screens down, below the paragraph and three lines of pills.
findings.who_objects: A visitor arriving on a phone from LinkedIn sees a face but not Mark's line or how to reach him without scrolling far. The brief asks for one message and one action on the first screen.

findings.where: Navigation: Profile, Articles, Blog, Contact and the home lockup (parts.txt p1–p5)
findings.fault: Every nav link points to '#'. A click never leaves the page, and 'Contact' does not even scroll to the email action on the same page.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who clicks 'Contact' or 'Articles' expecting to go somewhere gets no response.
